utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Baccard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume the cross-examination today, and I would like to tell you that the solemn declaration that you made is still in force, of course. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor. Good to see you back. Doctor, we left off several days ago talking a little bit about post-mortem and pre-mortem injuries. And in my discussion with you on that score, you noted in discussing your report which is P2314.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if I may, I think the doctor had a copy of his report prior to that. It may be expeditious if we could provide him with that so he could page through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we still have a hard copy, Mr. Margetts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, apologies, I don't have one to hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could -- if someone could provide. If not, then we will have to do it on the screen. But if someone has a copy available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will just search the other binders that we have with us, but I'm not hopeful at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, Mr. President, I will proceed. I think that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you provided, and if meanwhile someone tries to find a hard copy for Mr. Baccard. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, I noted during the course of your testimony, and this is on page 15794. At line 2, you noted that: "I believe that I must remind that you my report is a monitoring report, is a report of a monitor. I was present there in order to give my opinion on the quality of work undertaken by my Croat colleagues, and this is not an expertise report. This is a report drafted by an expert on the expertise that I did not carry out myself." Moving down a bit to line 10 -- 9: "So these are elements taken into account, but I, myself, did not have to make any -- make -- to make any this particular observation as to this. My report was rather -- internal report. It was made for the OTP, and I never thought, or did not think, that would be produced subsequently to the Chamber. This is not an expertise -- a report. I draft expert reports that are completely different. This is a technical report." If I can explore that commentary or testimony with you just a bit, Doctor. Do I understand you to say that the report that you had was merely pointing out different things that you observed during the course of these pathology examinations and other items that the Office of the Prosecutor might want to look into, but was not intended to substitute your opinion for the opinion of the pathologist who did the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the purpose of this report was to give my opinion as to the scientific validity of the reports made by the Croat experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, was your opinion intended to be taken by the Chamber as a substitute for the opinion rendered by the pathologists who did the autopsies?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I took part in this mission, in this observation mission, there was absolutely no intention at the moment of doing anything for the Trial Chamber. I was working for the OTP, as I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Maybe I wasn't clear in my question. You noted during the course of your testimony that if this had been an expert report, you would have done a much more detailed and thorough job. So my question for you is: Did your commentary, or did you intend your commentary on the work of the pathologists to be accepted by the Trial Chamber as a substitute for the opinion of the underlying pathologist, or the pathologist who did the autopsy?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I was clear in my answer either. When I took part in this mission, when I was in the observation mission, I did not have the Trial Chamber in mind at all because my report was for the OTP. It was a technical report for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir. So the answer to the question was your commentary meant to substitute for the opinion of the underlying pathologist, the answer to that question is, no, it was not intended. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is it not an accurate summary of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, maybe I'm not asking the question clearly enough. I'm not really -- maybe I'm not being doing well as it's being translated, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are several elements in your question, Mr. Kehoe, and that might confuse the witness. First of all, what kind of use to be made of his report in Court and how we should consider it is, of course, not for the witness to consider. Because whether it stays in the hands of the Office of the Prosecution, whether it's sent to the Court, whether the Court considers this to replace the expert opinion by those who performed the autopsies is not something I think -- that's what the witness explained to us, is not something was on his mind at the time. Therefore, I think you couldn't summarize the answer as you did, so please put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My sole intent, and I will move on, was just finding out exactly what the Trial Chamber is supposed to rely on for expert testimony or expert evidence that is being presented by -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We then try to cut this short. Mr. Baccard, was it your intention at the time to verify the scientific quality and merits of the autopsy performed by others and was not your role, that is not to say that your opinion would be -- would replace their opinion, but your opinion just gave an assessment of quality, reliability of -- mainly of the conclusions where you had not performed the autopsies yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, you didn't perform any of these autopsy, did you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this mission, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, if we can turn your attention to -- back to Dr. Clark's report. That's P1251.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can go to the fourth page of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the -- in the fourth paragraph down and under the heading deciding whether injuries found had occurred before or after death, Dr. Clark notes that: "Strictly speaking, therefore, in these decomposed and often incomplete bodies with no soft tissues in which to see bruising, and no body cavities in which to find internal bleeding or disrupted organs, it was virtually impossible to be certain that any injury found necessarily occurred in life, and theoretically all of them could have occurred after death, even the very obvious gun-shot injuries." Now, Doctor, of course, Dr. Clark is talking about basically skeletonized remains with no soft tissue and no body cavities to find internal bleeding. But with that information, do you agree with that statement presented to this Trial Chamber by Dr. Clark?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, regarding the difficulty of determining whether the wounds were anti-mortem or post-mortem on skeletal remains, yes, I must agree. It is very difficult to do so. But it's all a case-by-case system. Anyway you have to look at things on a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, shifting gears a bit to causes of injuries. Again, we've talked earlier about the fact that there was a significant passage of time involved here, and you were dealing with skeletonized remains many times. And would you agree, Doctor, that it was difficult, extremely difficult, to actually ascertain what the cause of injury actually was?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would have to refer to the reports. If I remember right, the bodies were in different states of conservation, sometimes they were putrefied, sometimes they were skeletal remains. I need to take a look at my report in order to answer because it does depend on the status of each body. I can't give a general answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's do that, Doctor. We'll explore some of the items that the Prosecutor has put on the clarification schedule as people who are killed, and will analyse those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can take a look at, first P1556. P1556. And, for the record, this is number 58 on the clarification schedule of bodies killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In this particular exhibit, as we go through the manner of death, there is, as can you see there, no signs of trauma, and the cause of injury is unknown. Now, in this particular instance, and I will tell you, Doctor, that just reading your three-line analysis of this, you say that -- and this is on page 66 of your report, which is P2314. In the spirit of expediency, Your Honour, if I can read three lines, as opposed to bringing it up on the screen, it may be quicker. "My notes are consistent with Dr. Definis-Gojanovic. The cause of death is unknown, and no data can be obtained from the examination of clothes and of the photograph taken after death." So with regard to this particular exhibit, and we have others there are quite of - we'll go through those - where it remained unknown, you agreed that the cause of death was unknown, as the underlying pathologist opined. So in this particular instance, for example, you cannot exclude death from natural cause, could you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, I don't have my report at hand, but I believe that what you have just read is exact. But thank you for giving me the report now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes. And, Doctor, and what I'm talking about, if you can turn to page 66 of your report. This is the -- your analysis of 04/011.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. So once again my question for you is in this -- because the cause of death is unknown, and for instance, there is no signs of trauma, you can't exclude death by natural causes, can you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't exclude any cause of death, just like my colleague did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're putting twice now the same question, even without putting that question. If the cause of death is unknown, this Chamber understands that it could be anything, including natural death and at least there are no signs, there's no trauma, so that's perhaps even more -- more likely or at least that it's an open possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think, Mr. President, with all due respect, and I agree with the chamber entirely, the question, of course, is why with these pathological reports being in the possession of the Prosecutor, we find these in the killing schedule that has been presented to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you think that this expert witness could answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think the answer to the question is, if in fact he says that with all of these -- and I have just a sampling of a half a dozen, and there are more. A sampling of these where the cause of death is unknown, and then he cannot exclude natural causes - in fact there is some in here that reflect natural causes - that they are -- obviously the Prosecution cannot prove that these were in fact killings and natural deaths. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... let's -- let's stick to what this expert can tell us. And he has told us, and I take it, Mr. Baccard, that would be true for the others as well, that if the cause of death is unknown that you could not exclude and there may even be signings for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, it may be helpful given that the rationale of the Prosecution is being raised by my learned friend. First to look at the specific example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it a matter that we can discuss in the presence of the witness or the expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... If you start interpreting what he ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, there are other matters in the autopsy report which are reflective of certain conclusions that may be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Something for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Possibly for re-examination, or since it is in evidence, I just invite my learned friend if he is going to be pursuing this line of cross-examination that he be inclusive in the references he makes to the indicia of killing in the reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have heard similar invitations from -- going from one side to the other. If Mr. Kehoe fails to do so, I'm quite confident that will you do it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with all due respect, I thought that Your Honour was asking me not to go through these unknowns because the witness could not exclude that manner of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you just want to stick to the unknowns, and that was what your questions were about at this moment, then Mr. Margetts at a later stage might find it interesting to look at other matters. And he is free to do so. Please proceed. But to ask the witness not only two times, but seven or eight times whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... an unknown cause of death means that you can't exclude death by natural causes, I think that's understood better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. President, I asked him twice, and I simply asked him the second time after the witness had the opportunity to review his report, as I'm sure the Chamber saw the courtroom deputy giving it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The next report is 1557. And for you, Dr. Baccard, it is 04/021. Again, if we put that on the screen, which is a P1557, this is a document that -- an autopsy that again notes that there are no visible signs of injuries. And if we could move to the -- the anthropological analysis, it notes that this person has been disabled for a long time. If we turn to page 2 of this, again, there is no evidence of any gun-shot wounds. And I believe in your report, on page 66, no particular remark can be done on this case because the cause of death remains undetermined. Again, we have a situation where cause of death from natural causes can not be excluded. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, regarding -- as far as forensics are concerned, no cause of death can be excluded, including natural death, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is another document that says no traces of injuries found on the body. The cause of death unascertained. I believe that ... your actual autopsy report is consistent with an unascertained cause of death. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my autopsy report but the autopsy report of Dr. Petrovecki. And regards the answers, I confirm that I agree with the fact that this cause of death was not ascertained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let me show you as part of this document, the information on the body that was contained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can ask to open X016-4905, and I do believe that additional translation is needed in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this is an information sheet, Doctor, that was -- I understand was provided to you when you were -- these bodies were being examined, and subsequently it was made a part of this file. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall having seen a file of this type regarding the identification of the body of this victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see similar reports such as this?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: A file of this type or a report of this type, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So I take it if we can just scroll down on this sheet for this person, so I take it that you didn't see, for instance, in line 13 where determined or supposed cause of death is the natural cause of death.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not my recollection, no. I do not recall having seen this document, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to P1555. P1555. And you examined this on page 34, I believe, of your report. We have the anthropological report and the autopsy is -- it says no visible signs of injury, and the cause of death is unknown. Now, in your actual report, you note that basically to paraphrase what you have, since a bullet was found in the pants, that the gun-shot wound -- that you could hypothesize, or these facts suggest that the victims contained gun-shots possibly concerning the soft tissues. This is it only a hypothesis. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with regard to that the actual cause of death in this remains unknown because you couldn't view any organ damage for this body to come to any final conclusion on this, other than the fact that given there are no visible signs of injury, we can't make a determination on cause of death.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will have to specify my answer. With regard to the forensic analysis, the body was partially putrefied and partly skeletonized, and this did not allow to us see which were the traumatic lesions on the body. So I have to answer if I base my answer on the analysis of the body there was no traumatic lesions that was visible. However upon examining the body, we were also able to examine the clothing and the secondary examination which followed which is the examination of the clothes which was done in the presence of the forensic pathologist as I explained at the beginning. We found a presence of a fragment of a projectile as well as some tears that showed that there was a defect created by the projectile. An entry point was found at the pant level, and this is why in my report I talked about this hypothesis. I said that it is a hypothesis, that it is only a hypothesis consistent with a gun-shot wound, but there is absolutely no certainly, and I leave it up to the Trial Chamber to draw their own -- its own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But as you sit here today, you are not changing the underlying autopsy conclusion that this cause of death is unknown, are you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered this question, and my answer was slightly nuanced. If you wish I could explain it to you again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next one, P1551.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I believe in your report, Doctor, it is the bottom of page 91. Now, Doctor, P1551 again is an uncertain death. And during -- if we look at the summary of this autopsy, it says: "Probable fracture of the left side of the pelvis, partial rib factures. It is hard to say when this damage, these damages occurred." Now, this is it an example, is it not, Doctor, of the difficulty of ascertaining injuries that are either post-mortem or ante-mortem, isn't?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct in this particular case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in this case, of course, as with the others, you can't exclude natural causes as a cause of death. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, as I already explained earlier, if or when the cause of death is under determined, one has to take into account the possibility of a natural death as well. We cannot exclude that cause, just like we cannot exclude other causes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, could I seek some clarification. Dr. Baccard, sometimes we see "cause of death unknown." In other reports we see "unascertained." Is there any meaning in this different -- difference of language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my mind, no. There are no differences. It really depends on the style of the forensic pathologist. Some people may use one term and others may use another term. But as far as I'm concerned the use of those two terms is very similar, and that's anonymous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Doctor, the last one in the series --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, I didn't mean to cut the Chamber off, if there was a follow-up question. The last in this series is P1561.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I believe that you are -- that your opinion on that is at the -- or your statement on that is at the bottom of page 104. I think you note some discrepancies with some of the statements concerned post-mortem injuries. But if we look back at the autopsy report on the screen. Again, we have a situation where there were signs of injuries and at least one post-mortem injury on the right facial bone and with no other known death -- excuse me, known cause of death. Again without repeating what we did before with this, other than the minor additions or commentary you make to Dr. Strinovic's report. Again we have one that is unknown, where the cause of death by natural causes cannot be excluded. That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move on. Let us move on to the actual cause of death and some of the difficulties presented in getting to the cause of death. And if I can, if I can turn back to Dr. Clark's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, that is P1251, on page 5 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As this is coming up, Doctor, when you were working for the Office of the Prosecutor and doing this commentary, did you have anything to do with putting together this scheduled list of killings that the Prosecutor has submitted to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 5 of this document, and in the -- under the area of deciding on the significance of the injuries found and whether they were the cause of death, under number 4, under that bold, it says: "In this respect" -- it's the second paragraph under the bold in the middle. "In this respect it has be realized it is not the damage to the bones themselves that kills people, but rather the associated damage to surrounding tissues and internal organs. With most of the latter missing in these cases, it was therefore seldom possible to strictly prove a precise cause of death, only to imply it." Now, do you agree with that statement, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must nuance this answer as well. And especially when we read the first sentence mentioned by my colleague, Dr. John Clark. The lesions inflicted to the human bones may be fatal because the internal cavity of the bones is the seat of a -- marrow which is in blood, and this can be a cause of hemorrhage and that can be fatal. So this being said, I confirm what is written in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so if we take this one step further, Doctor, when we're doing these types of pathological examinations and autopsies, there is a relatively high degree of speculation on the part of the pathologist when he or she is trying to come up with the actual cause of death. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speculation is not the right term that I would use. I would rather use the word scientific deduction. When you have a point of entry, which is situated on the arch of a rib, for instance, and when you can see also an exit point on the opposite rib, and if we know that the heart is between those two points, the entry point and the exit point, the scientific deduction which is the not a speculation allows us to conclude that the projectile transfers or crossed the organ which was between those two ribs. It's a deduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, sir, and, of course, this is not the type of deduction that you would normally make in your practice as a forensic pathologist when you're examining bodies, for instance, for the French authorities back home or in a similar venue when you're making a determination on the cause of death, looking at a relatively fresh body?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have at our disposal other means and those means are -- for instance we have to examine the body and the soft tissues. But this is part of the scientific reasoning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, one of the things that you have in other circumstances -- other instances to come up with a cause of death, you often times have information on the actual manner of death, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand very well your question. Do you mean that we have information coming from other body parts that are present when we carry out our autopsy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm talking about information, Doctor, that -- concerning the actual place where there was located -- or where the body was recovered. For instance, information such as, was this body at a front line position in a trench? Or was this body found in the middle of a minefield? Information like that, that would assist you in coming to a determination on the cause of death. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the forensic practice, which is the current forensic practice in France or in other countries, we do have the first elements of the investigation when we carry out an autopsy, but in the sites for which I took part as an observer, I did not have those information -- that information, precise information, with regard to each of the victim, and an investigation had not been carried out in that way. We were not informed of these elements at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if we look at -- let's look at P1554. And, for instance this is an individual who, according to the autopsy report, is dressed in a military uniform. This autopsy says most likely an explosive injury to the head. You note your autopsy that it was a gun-shot. But in a situation such as this, regardless of the actual cause of death, none of your analyses discount that this is a -- a cause of death or injuries that resulted from actual combat. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I was not able to know what were the circumstances surrounding the death. I could only see the cause of deaths but not the circumstances of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Doctor, and I guess that would take us one step past combat because you can't -- don't know the circumstances. You wouldn't, for instance, know if this person died from friendly fire or enemy fire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, is it really something that an expert should tell this Chamber, whether, if you get a partly saponified body, that this witness could tell us whether it was friendly fire if in combat or enemy fire. Is this really something you consider to be within the -- and having listened to the very, very precise answers of this expert, would you really expect him to say, Well, of course, you could say it is friendly fire or this. On the basis of the autopsy, Dr. Baccard, I take it, that your answer would be in the negative, that you couldn't make any distinction between whether it was in combat or not, as you said before. So if you can't determine whether it was in combat yes or no, I take that you could not tell us that if it was in combat, that it was -- whether it was friendly fire or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour, I was not there while everything was unfolding, and so this is not something that an expert witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just for the record, Mr. President, what I'm actually doing is -- and I know Your Honour understands this, but I'm trying to make a record, not only for the Trial Chamber but for anybody else that looks at this, to try and go through facts and circumstances that may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, if you are before a jury, address the -- make a record for the jury. If you are before a professional Bench, make a record for the professional Bench who have to determine the matters before it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, that is, by way of clarification, that's what I'm trying to do, make a record for this. So I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The other issues, just on this score, if we can turn to P1546. I'm going show you two exhibits on this. P1546 for you, Doctor, is 04/016. This is a female that was -- died, it looks like from explosive injuries. And these are actually parts of a female, if I'm correct. Because it is 04016 BP, so as opposed to a body, these are body parts, where it reflects that it was explosive injury and the actual underlying documents note that the clothing was burnt. And I believe in your report on page 69 you say that this is consistent with an explosive device.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn to P1668.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask questions about both of these together. That is 03009 for you, Doctor. This is unusual in the sense that this is a body that was wrapped in a blanket. I believe you note that on page 50 of your report. And likewise in this item we had some burning on the flesh of this individual. Now, in both of these, Doctor, were these consistent with -- these injuries, and both of these consistent with someone walking into a minefield and stepping on a mine?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot answer that question. In this particular case, I can only describe the lesions, I can only attribute a cause to these lesions, but it is very difficult for me to explain the circumstances in which this occurred because I don't have sufficient elements for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when you say death by explosion, it could be any type of explosion; mines, tank fire, artillery fire. Any of the above. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Insofar as there is no shrapnel inside the body or in the soft tissues, we cannot analyse the shrapnels, so, therefore, we cannot know where they come from. It is very difficult to answer this question. The way the lesions are shown or distributed on the body can give us a clue and can -- can make us believe that there was an explosion. If you have an explosion of a mine, if you step on a mine, then the inferior members are going to be affected, and then the lesions will go from the lower body -- from the lower parts, lower limbs, to the head, but if we don't have shrapnel inside the body, embedded, we cannot really make any conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted, and I did too, a mine that was stepped on. Of course, you're familiar with other mines that are triggered by wiring, are you not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And, likewise, going through these autopsies, you could not exclude that there was criminal violence from one person on another, even one Serb person on another Serb person, could you? Let's take an example, and I will show you one. I will be probably easier that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to P1685.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: For you, Doctor, it is G 06/24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I would like to see whether we can get an answer, but I will rephrase your last question. Dr. Baccard, if you do not know the ethnicity of the victim and if you do not know the ethnicity of someone who may have played a role in the cause of death, then you couldn't exclude that it was one Serb killing another Serb, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, I have no scientific criteria that allow me to determine the ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can take a look at P1685.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is a report that the autopsy initially comes out with an explosion to the head and trunk injury -- explosive head and trunk injuries. And you disagree because of pellets that are likely fired from a shotgun. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Now, two things about that, with regard to the explosive. The first question I have for you is: Was it your rationale that this was, for instance, not a mine or hand-grenade because of the pellets?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the fragment, the foreign parts, this was lead pellets as used in ammunition of the hunting rifle type --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I may have missed where this case appears in the report of Dr. Baccard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is it on page 99 of his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page, Mr. President. And my apologies for not pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you familiar with mines in the former Yugoslavia that had contained in them little steal balls that were triggered and fired out on assaulting troops. Are you familiar with those?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a specialist in weapons and ammunitions. I'm speaking of projectiles that were highlighted during the autopsy and that have visible in X-rays were not pellets but small spheres such as those used in hunting rifles with multiple projections. These were -- pellets for me is a flat geometric form. These were small spheres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Like small balls. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Small balls, I don't recall the dimension, but 2 millimetres or 1.5 to 2 millimetres. They're visible on the photographs. Some were embedded in the bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you 1D00-0763, if I may. And this is a recognition handbook that was put together by the Canadian authorities. And is says -- if we can just go to the front page and blow that up just a bit. That's the front page, Doctor, of this recognition handbook, and this is a book that has various types of armaments. And I have annexed a page. If we can turn to the next page, and just bring that down a little bit. This is it an MRUD anti-personnel mine that -- if you notice at the type of the kill, it is a fragmentation effect with 650 steal balls in it, strung together when it is triggered. Are you familiar with this type of mine, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again I have to say that I'm not a weapons specialist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll to offer 1D00-0763 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1310, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Kehoe, it may have been clear from the answer of this expert that the size of the steel balls might play a role. If there would be any information in relation to the size of the 650 steel balls, that certainly assist the Chamber in following the -- the possible explanation you have suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, and I was hoping the witness could help that. I don't know, but I will find out yet further. As an officer of the court, I have to tell you, I don't know the size of those balls, as to whether or not they are consistent with the actual steel balls that the witness found or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, it was not steel, this was led. These were -- these were led spheres, not steal spheres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not iron, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you -- Dr. Baccard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, just moving ahead through this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that this was a -- these -- it says pellets in your English report, but I guess the lead balls that you saw were fired by a shotgun. And my question to you is, you know that that's -- a shotgun is not a weapon that's normally carried by a soldier. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the equipment, the weapons equipment of the -- of the forces that were on the ground at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on your experience in the former Yugoslavia and doing this type of work for the OTP, you would agree with me that a shotgun is, based on your experience, not a weapon that is normally carried by soldiers, is it?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that in my experience I have encountered in some cases that it's difficult for me to assess precisely this type of injury, but I don't feel competent to answer the question as to whether they are part of the standard issue of a military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us take this one step further, and you correct me if I'm wrong, I think I tried to go through these autopsies with some degree of diligence, but pardon me if I didn't. But I do believe that is the only instance in your autopsies that have been presented, and I do believe that there are 53 of them where a shotgun is a weapon that you conclude or opine was the weapon used to shoot the projectiles that caused the death. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's the only case or whether I found it in another cases. What I can say is that this type of injury is a type of injury that we frequently come across in civilian practice. It's a type of injury that I know well. I would also add that assuming we would think that it's an explosive device, that disseminated the small balls, this lead shot, we would have on clothing very different appearance. In the event of a firing of these signal lead pellets or balls with a shotgun, the flow is by a barrel, it has a certain shape. And in terms of the distance from the target, we would have on the clothing a wide tear with small peripheral pellets, but if we're thinking of the explosion of a device, we would see dissemination at the outset and a multitude of small impacts on the clothing which wasn't the case in this particular file.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Your answer, just triggered something in my mind, and it is the first, you know, first two lines of page 24 -- excuse me, page 24, line 10 and 11 you say: "What I can say that this is the type of injury" -- excuse me. "That this type of injury is the type of injury that we frequently come across in civilian practice." As an expert let me have you assume certain facts. The Prosecutor has charged that this death occurred -- and this at number 290 of their clarification schedule. Has occurred on the 5th of August, of 1995. Likewise assume that the evidence in this Chamber is that there were no Croatian soldiers in Donji Lapac on the 5th of August, 1995. Based on that, sir, would that be consistent of -- with your statement that you just gave, that this would be the type of weapon you would see in civilian practice and you could rationally conclude that this was done in a civilian setting as well on the 5th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I consider the sentence that the sentence regarding the fact that Dr. Baccard has substantial experience in this type of examination, he has seen these types of injuries before, cannot be equated or should not be taken out of context and placed with this hypothetical scenario. It is distorting the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has shown several times to know exactly where the limits of his expertise are, and we will hear from him whether he can answer your question or not, Mr. Kehoe. Dr. Baccard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, absolutely not. The reference that I was making to the unexceptional nature of this type of injury in my forensic civilian forensic practice was only aimed at indicating that I was used to seeing this sort of injury. And that if I wrote that it was related to a shot fired with lead pellet projectile, that this is something that I was basing on my experience. Any other assumption or conclusion drawn from that sentence would be erroneous, and I'm not competent either to speak to the nationality of the soldiers present at a particular point or as to the date, that's totally foreign to my area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move on to some of the analyses that -- or some of the discussion in your report that goes back to the autopsies as they pertain to explosions or blast injuries. And I note just on some of these -- that some of the autopsies in your opinions. And you note on -- at least six occasions, and I think it's more than that, in P1546, P1549, P1559, P1568, and P1544, that individuals died from explosions and blast injuries. And I believe that you concurred with that assessment. And trust me, Doctor, I went through, and I went through all of those, and you in fact didn't concur. But my interest -- and if we can just take one for example, just go to P1546 which is 05010 for you. Now, this is a blast injury, and I believe in page 81 of your report you agree with the conclusions, and I think you told us you can't tell us anything about the circumstances of death. And the Prosecutor has alleged --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, it is now for the second time that you say that the cause of death was, where the report says probably. Would you please be as precise as the witness is, that what is the probable cause of death is not the same as what is a determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Judge. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I said that, Judge, simply because I was looking from a different item than the exhibit that was on the screen, and that is -- I should be looking at P1549. My apologies. That's on the screen now. It is 0510.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the Chamber is 100 percent correct, this is -- you know, all probable causes of death notwithstanding causes of death, it is all probable. But, Doctor, with regard to something like this, I mean it is impossible for you to say when this death occurred. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer solely on the basis of the first page of the report. Would it be possible to move to the description of injuries?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sure.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 2 or page 3. May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. In this case it was perfectly possible to answer regarding the fact that these injuries did indeed take place before death. They were ante-mortem. There was soft tissue. There was a metal fragment, shrapnel, that was included in the soft tissues. And the various fractures noted by the Croatian expert confirmed that there was signed of hemorrhaging and, therefore, ante-mortem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question -- if I could take it one step further, Doctor, and I'm not disputing your conclusions nor the underlying pathologist's conclusions on this score. And my point then is on this particular issue. That -- and this is at 48 of the clarification schedule, I do believe -- excuse me, 49 of the clarification schedule, that the clarification schedule notes that the body was killed on 24 August 1995. And my question for you, Doctor, is that you cannot say whether or not it occurred there or some earlier date or some date after that, can you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to another one of these reports, P1544, 65 ter 6076. That's 07/022. And that's on page 116 of your report. Now, this is an individual that -- if you look at the first summary of the autopsy report, under the clothing, it notes that the clothing torn remains of a military olive green shirt with epaulettes nylon underpants with blue/grey stripes. Now, Doctor, when you saw that type of information, did you and the other team conclude that this person was in fact or had been a soldier?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The type of clothing was mentioned as being military clothing, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Doctor. But on the assessment as to whether or not this person was in fact a soldier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I think the witness clearly says that what he observes is the type of clothing whether that was an actor playing in a war movie, whether that was civilian clothes in military uniform, whether it was someone who had just been demobilized, I think the witness clearly said, and he is very strict in these matters, that he observes facts, and he did not draw any conclusions. When he says, I observed that this was clothing of a military type, that is all. That's a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge. But the question is, and I think the Chamber wants to know, is when you were looking at this, given the -- well, let me take it one step further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but let's stick to what the expertise of the witness is. And I think the witness is -- I'm quite happy to see that, he is very strict in his answers, what is within and what is not within his expertise. And whether -- how this material was used by others, and whether they say, You see from the clothing that it is an actor or not an actor or a soldier, that's not -- neither within the expertise, nor within the limits of the responsibility of this expert witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do beg to differ. And I will ask this question of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you make assessments during the course of your examinations that certain individuals that you would -- examining had been soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they were wearing military clothing or civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you make that assessment? If they were in military clothing, they were soldiers; if they were this civilian clothing, they were, in your mind, civilians?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that must be in my report. There was a table indicating the number of people wearing predominantly military clothing, and I believe I indicated that in a paragraph in the preamble to the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Going to this particular issue on this particular examination, would you have concluded that this person was a soldier given the fact that he was wearing a military olive green shirt with epaulettes?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the criteria that were -- in the assessment of the overall results of this mission, the status was affirmed only when there were several items of clothing or typical items of -- of uniform that were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So let's turn to this particular autopsy. Did you consider this person who was wearing this type of shirt to be a soldier?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer. It appears in my notes, and I -- I can't refer to those notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, were you told when you were to those examinations that virtually every male, Serbian male in the Krajina from 18 to possibly even higher than 60 years of age was in fact pressed into service as a soldier? Were you told that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No such thing was said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you ever told that soldiers leaving the front line - not saying all of them - that soldiers leaving the front line discarded their uniforms and put on civilian clothing as they began to leave the area? Were you told that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, I was told very little when I went on this monitoring mission. I had very little information which -- to a certain extent I deplore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you saying, sir, that you would have wanted more information as you were looking through this, but you weren't given that information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- One question first, Dr. Baccard, before you answer the question, if need be, of Mr. Kehoe. Did you ever consider what the status of a person was? Or did you rather observe what he was wearing at the time without drawing any conclusions as being beyond what is within your expertise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is certain that the criteria used to classify a person depending on the clothing worn in one category or another is -- uses limited criteria because very often the clothes are torn, they are in a poor state. But what was is concluded, and this is stated in the preamble to my report, to indicate that a person was military was to have at least two items of military uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so you considered him to be clothed in military attire. But did you consider whether someone was or was not a soldier, or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. But I had no way of determining that. That is why I clearly indicated at the beginning of my report what the criteria we used to classify these people in one group or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just finishing with this particular exhibit, Doctor, and looking at your report, and I think the cause of death is most likely explosive injuries, and you can't tell us if this was tank fire, mortar fire, booby-traps, artillery, or whatever, can you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let us move to another exhibit where in fact you disagree with the assessment made by the forensic pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That would be P1678. 65 ter 6042.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in your volume it is, 03/010. And I will get the page for you, Doctor. That would be on page 51 of your report. Now, in the actual underlying autopsy it says gun-shot or explosive injuries of both shanks. And I believe in your report you noted that it was -- a cause of death is undetermined. That's in the last line of your report. Just looking at this, Doctor, when you changed or you offered a different opinion, if I may, other than that put forth by Dr. Blazanovic, did you examine this body, or did you just examine the photographs? What was the basis of your difference of opinion. I note that in your report you looked at some photographs.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, of course, present during the course of the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have some discussion with Dr. Blazanovic at the time regarding how you might have seen this differently or come to a different conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all probability. But I don't really recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So taking that probability, what we have in this instance is two individuals -- two experienced -- or pathologists coming to a difference of an opinion when examining a corpse. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What we have here simply, Doctor, is two pathologists looking at a particular body and coming to different conclusions --

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to move into other subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I'm looking at the clock at this moment. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Half an hour, 45 minutes, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, after the break, you have 25 minutes left. And the Chamber encourages you, and I know that I'm now exaggerating, not to put questions to the witness of the kind, Is it true that you couldn't conclude from the striped under wear what the level of education of that person was, or questions like, If you say red, you exclude that it was green, that type of questions really are totally superfluous. That is also why the Chamber limits you to 25 minutes after the break, and I tried to put you on the right track several times during the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if i can, I would like to comment on Mr. President's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said I was exaggerating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge. I understand. But it was more than exaggeration, and I would like some commentary on that score. And I can do it now, or I can do it after the break, as Your Honour so pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will see whether we find time to hear your comments on that matter, and I will discuss it with my colleagues. We will have a break, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you asked to be able to comment. The Chamber will not deprive you of that opportunity, but, at the end of the testimony of the witness, not earlier. And you have 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm grateful for having that opportunity. I want to make my position clear to the Chamber and comment on your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, if we can go back and discuss some of the testimony we just were talking about in P1678, an instance where you offered a different opinion on the cause of death from a gun-shot or explosion to undetermined. I want to talk to you a little bit about a situation where we have the converse, in the sense that the cause of death is initially -- is initially listed as undetermined or unknown, excuse me, and you have changed -- you offer a different hypothesis, that it's a gun-shot or an explosion. And the first exhibit on that score is P1566. In your book, sir, it is G07/026, page 120. And I will go through these two different autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go to P1566 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is the situation where the cause of death is offered as unknown. And you note in your last line of your report at 120 that the hypothesis of injury by explosion cannot be excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The other item, other exhibit on this score is P1555, 65 ter 6034.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Likewise, and this, it is a cause of death that is unknown. Again, Doctor, it's 02/009 for your reference point, and I will get you the page. It's on page 34 of this document of your report. Where you order that the last line: "These facts suggest that the victim sustained gun-shot possibly concerning the soft tissues. This is only a hypothesis." Now, once again, Doctor, we have two different opinions. I take it you were at the autopsies when both of these were conducted in Zagreb, yet two pathologists offer different opinions on the cause of death and come to two different conclusions, as we can see. Doctor, that, of course, renders the scientific certainty regarding these causes of death somewhat how, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not entirely sure that the conclusions, the ultimate conclusions can be said -- can be characterized in the way my learned friend has characterized them. The expert certainly refers to hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The witness can certainly explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact -- I think in the first example it was clear that there was a hypothesis, and that, in the second one, as well, so the witness can -- So half, you're right; half, you're wrong, Mr. Margetts. Please continue, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe there was a hypothesises in both of them. And I may stand corrected, on page 120 of the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but you mentioned once that it was a hypothesis, and I think you didn't mention that for the second one. You are talking about different conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise. The second one on page 34, my learned friend could look at the last line, and that suggested cause of death, also said this is only hypothesis. That is for P1555, the actual exhibit that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Doctor, my question to you is the same. When you look at these and you offer a different hypothesis, does not -- does your hypothesis or offering a different way to look at this, render the scientific conclusions as to the cause of death low?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I noted very specifically that I was only offering a hypothesis on both cases. Very early on when we performed the autopsy --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: When the autopsy was performed. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... there was a discussion among the pathologists. But I was there, during the entire steps of the expertise including the examination of the clothing, and the pathologists had not present for that. And I still believe that checking the clothes is extremely important to be able to ascertain the causes of death because the clothes are around the body, and the clothes can testify to a number of things. They can -- there can be torn, you can see bleeding also on the clothes, and this can help interpret in a certain way what the -- with a was found in the autopsy, and this is exactly what happened in the two cases that you mentioned, in G02/009 and G07/026. I believe that's the one. In the first case G02/009 B, inside the trousers I found a fragment of -- project of the fragmented bullet nose in the trousers, and checking -- we checked the clothes. Well, I was present when the clothes were checked. First they were cleaned, and I could really see that there were tears that were very specific. And it was not just in one layer of clothes, it was on several layers of clothes. When there is a tear, well, sometimes you can give it very relative value, but when you have the same tear on several layers of clothes, for example, in the trousers and the underpants, then you know this is more suspect. And then on top of that you find a piece of projectile inside. I think that scientifically you can offer this hypothesis. With the reservation of course that this is only a hypothesis and that there is no certainty attached to it. But I believe that the legal experts have to be informed that these findings were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Doctor, I'm disagreeing with you that an anthropological examination of the clothing is important. But my next step is given you were there and you examined the clothing and you were there when Dr. Definis-Gojanovic in P1566, G07/026, conducted that autopsy, and in P1555 when Davor Strinovic conducted that autopsy, did you, after you examined this clothing at the scene, go back and talk to these particular physicians and express to them the concerns and ask them to take them into consideration so that the pathology report, the autopsy report would be as accurate as possible? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember specifically for both cases. But it's true that on -- in some cases I went back to my colleagues to just tell them about what findings had been made and when the clothes were checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when they -- you gave them that position, can you tell us in what instance you did that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on that information, did the forensic pathologist take that information and take it into consideration in filing his other her autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some cases, no, since we have a discrepancy in the written report, as we just saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So going back full circle, Doctor. When we look at these particular items where you offer hypothesis on a different conclusion, are you saying that your opinion is right and the underlying examination pathologist is wrong? Or are you saying that these are just two different opinions?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In cases like the one that we're talking about, the two that we're talking about, these opinions are different. I'm not ascertaining with certainty that the cause of death was either an explosion or a gun-shot wound. All I'm saying is that after having been there when the clothes were checked, especially for G07/026, after having checked the photography for this one, the photography that was taken right after the -- closely after death, scientifically there is a possibility of raising other hypothesises. But these remain hypothesis and have absolutely no certainty attached to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Let me just conclude with one short area as my time is short. And we have another situation where looking at various autopsy reports, the initial autopsy, cause of death was most probably explosion or blast, and then you offered a different hypothesis of gun-shots. And I will put before the Chamber those numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Those, Doctor, are autopsies where their initial cause of death was most likely an explosion or a blast, and you changed to a hypothesis of gun-shot. Without what repeating exactly what we went through before, if I asked you the same questions with regard to these particular autopsies, Doctor, where you offer a different hypothesis, it would be just that, your hypothesis, and would that be again other occasions where you say there is a scientific possibility of raising other hypothesises - I'm reading page 38, lines 6 and 7 - these remain hypothesises and have absolutely no certainty attached to them. Would that -- your answer be the same on the hypothesis that you rendered when you changed these results from gun-shot blast or explosions to gun-shots, would that be the same? That those conclusions would remain simply hypothesises and no certainty attaches to them?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first, I didn't modify the conclusions of my colleagues. My colleagues took their own responsibility, of course, and wrote the conclusions that they drew and signed their report. I'm not going to modify anything. However, I can highlight my point of view and present my point of view, and I consider that it is scientifically validated. But I can't give you a general answer on all these cases that are on the screen. I have to look at them on a case-by-case basis in order to back what I said. You know, to tell you for this one, this is a certainty; for this one, this is a hypothesis and nothing more, when I differ with the conclusion drawn by the Croat pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, and my time is short, and so if I can just get through this and ask you, if it is a hypothesis, there is it no certainty attached to it, but you do have occasion where you just outright disagree with the forensic pathologist's conclusion. And it is it more than hypothesis; it's certainty in your mind?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. But in such cases -- here, this is it a very general answer. I'm not talking about specific cases. When you -- when you have an expertise that's comprehensive with examination of the body, X-rays, checking the clothes, when you do all these processes, all these steps, I believe you have more elements at hand than when you're limited to just the examination of the body or the skeletal remains. The traditional cases where there was a discrepancy between my conclusions and the conclusions drawn by my colleagues were mainly for -- were for corpses where the expert had believed that it was an explosion that was the cause of death. But as far as I'm concerned, based on the X-rays and based on the clothes that I had looked at as well as photographs, I could provide new elements, other elements. Which were they? Regarding the X-rays it was -- when you have a projectile that is fragmented, the tears are going to be very different, the impact are going to be very different than when have you the shrapnel that create lesions. Why is that? Because the projectile is a different speed. It's very high for those who come from an AK-47, for example, but when it's a fragment that is projected either by a grenade or mine or a shell, then the speed is much lower. Then there's also the different in the nature of the metal used in the projectile. Thirdly, when you look at X-rays, with a body that is full of shrapnel -- is full of fragments coming from a mine, this is very different than when you have a body with a projectile was fragmented. For example, a thigh that has been hit by a bullet. What is it going to happen there? From the entry wound, you will have broken bone, the broken femur and then we'll have a cloud, a snow cloud, you know, because of the -- because the first the projectile hits the bone and then is scattered. So if we have an X-ray with a person that has been shot by explosion and fragmented, the fragmentation can be seen from the entry wound. All these fragments enter everywhere in the body, so you can't mix -- there is no confusion possible. There is no -- you can't mix things up. Then secondly, regarding the clothes, it's the same thing for the clothes. Somebody who is hit by a grenade, with fragments of grenades, you will have a number of entry wounds and several defects on the body, whereas if the person is first hit by a projectile that fragments inside the body will have one entry wound and then everything will be scattered on the way out. So there is different steps and -- that are very important when you examine a body. And depriving yourself either voluntarily or involuntarily of the information you can get from one of the steps, whether X-ray, whether it's the clothes check, is going to place the expert in a situation where he has less information at hand to draw his conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, quickly because my time is running short, let us look at one exhibit on the list of exhibits that I just discussed and that would be P1573, 65 ter 6060. For your purposes, it is on page 97, G06/012 B. This notes, probably an explosive injury to the head. If we go to the next page and we look at the fluoroscopy examination. Down a little bit, point E. Thank you. It notes, post-mortem remains mixed with dirt, stones showing only a head without fractures. There is no mandible or any other metallic objects. In analysing this, Doctor, where it says probably an explosive injury, you offer on page 97 yet a different conclusion without any metallic or fluoroscopy objects -- any metallic objects seen during the fluoroscopy examination that the location of the injuries and their aspect appear to be do more likely to a gun-shot coming from the right, rather than an explosion. Now, is that a conclusion that you're making there, Doctor, or is that again a hypothesis to be considered?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no certainty attached to this. I say that it appears to be more likely due. So there is two reservations here. Saying that with my experience I would tend to favour the hypothesis of a gun-shot wound, rather than an explosion wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... using that word, that statement by you on page 97, is a hypothesis as well.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I feel it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we try to -- because we're talking about hypothesis, we are talking about likelihood. Dr. Baccard, is my understanding right, and I'm -- take you through a couple of situations, that if the expert concludes that no cause of death can be established, that when you come with a hypothesis, that what you're actually saying is that you found indicators which give an explanation at a level of probability or likelihood but without certainty, where the indicators are strong enough to express that likelihood or probability, and then you call it a hypothesis. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second situation, where the expert comes to a conclusion, probable or likely, if you give a competing hypothesis or a competing likelihood, do I understand that you say that the indicators you have observed cause you to give another probable cause of death, although without certainty, different from the probable or likely cause of death expressed by the other expert, because you find the indicators more favouring your explanation than they do favour the explanation of the expert who wrote the autopsy report. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. If I may, just -- can I make a small comment in relation to the case we had looked at, just to give you an example of how we worked. Right before the break, we were talking about a case where it was the opposite situation. My colleague concluded that the death probably came from an explosion or gun-shot; whereas I said that according to my logic, it was impossible to ascertain the cause of death. Why is that? Because I think the lesions there were on part of a limb, peripheral limb, and no major blood vessel is in that limb. So we can both agree on the fact that there was a wound to the wrist, but it is not because have you been hit by a bullet with a wrist that you're go doing die of it. Because you can survive if you just have a wrist injury. Sow need to have very certain reasons on what caused the death, but also when you look at all the injuries, you have to make sure that maybe these injuries actually injured a vital organ. So when you're an expert, you have to be very strict in your reasoning, and this is why sometimes we come to different conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just gave then, therefore, at least if I understood you well, is that where apparently your colleague found that indicators would justify an expression of probability, you thought that these indicators would not justify to express such a probable cause of death, and that, therefore, you had to conclude that it was -- and that, therefore, you had to conclude that it was an unknown cause of death. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I -- there was an interruption in the translation, and I heard you in English somewhat, but I couldn't follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can read it on your screen, I think this -- what I started with is the example you just gave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my answer is yes. Given the probable location of the wound, because this wound was not on a vital organ, and it was impossible to say that the cause of death was in relation to this or that, because we had no element that would allow us to affirm this, to be absolutely sure of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And not even strong enough to express a probable cause of death.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it could be possible. But when parts of the body is missing, which was the case here, or when you have no more soft tissue, with soft tissue that were probably involved in the trajectory of the projectile, when there is nothing left, it's very difficult to be affirmative in one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm actually out of time, Doctor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course the time I took, Mr. Kehoe, is not deduced from your -- of course if you're done with your question that is fine, but I try to be fair in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do appreciate that. I will try to wrap up within the next minute or so. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The bottom line with all of your conclusions where you offer different opinions, different hypothesises, different ways of looking at this evidence, you are doing just that, aren't you, Doctor?
