Offering the Office of the Prosecutor a different way to look at this examination or to look at this evidence while offering no certainty to the conclusions or to the statement -- the scientific certainty to the conclusions you put forth in your report. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with you fully. There are some scientific conclusions that were absolutely certain, and the majority of the reports and upon examination of the bodies, we agreed with my -- I agreed with my colleagues, my colleagues -- my Croat colleagues and myself were in agreement for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, thank you very much for your time, and I appreciate you coming back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Baccard, you dealt in the last few minutes with the issue of certainty, probability, hypothesis, the various indicators that you take into account to reach conclusions. My question is: When there is a finding that the cause of death is unknown, does that mean that there were no indicators of a cause of death; or does that mean that you were unable to reach a sufficient level of certainty to ascribe a cause of death?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The second part of your sentence is quite right, and it is illustrated by the discrepancy in the opinion that I mentioned. It is not because at some parts you can see lesions which show that there was a gun-shot injury, in a peripheral limb for instance, that that will be or that this will be reason to affirm that the person died from a gun-shot. You must have a vital organ that's touched or that's injured by this bullet or a gun-shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Right. So it is -- there could be indicators of a cause of death, but your finding could still be that the cause of death is unknown.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Baccard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Court has no questions, is there any need for further questions to the witness based on what Mr. Margetts just raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's true for all three Defence teams. Mr. Kehoe, since we have now concluded the testimony of the witness, I don't know whether the comments you would like to make are of a kind which still could have any impact on what happens at this moment in court. If not, I would first like to excuse the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine. My comments are directed to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This concludes your evidence, Dr. Baccard. [Interpretation] Thank you very much for coming to testify not only once, but twice before us, and I wish you a safe return even though if it is not too far.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you have an opportunity. What I did before the break, perhaps to make that clear, that unanimously the Chamber was of the opinion that your questions were sometimes repetitious, and sometimes the questions and the answers did not assist the Chamber, and that's what I expressed. And when I say "your questions," of course I mean to say, "many of your questions." That's what I tried to express before the break. Please have a short moment to comment, if there's any need to comment, and may I remind that you this still a Court of law and not a debating club. So I'm not seeking any debate, but we would not deprive you from a possibility to put on the record what you think you need to say. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I take great umbrage at Your Honour's comments. I also object strenuously to being restricted on a time with a witness such as this. There has been 189 murders, killings, not murders, killings added to this. The Office of the Prosecutor has added heaven knows how many unknown uncertain matters there. I addressed some of them today. And the question for the Defence is, without guidance from this Chamber as to how the appellant decision is going to be rendered, how is the Defence supposed to represent our respective clients? The only way to do that is to systematically try to go through these particular autopsies in topic area. I didn't go through 189; I took selected areas of that. Now we have to answer to that without some other information coming from the Chamber. And we cannot stand idlely by and allow the Prosecution to put forth unsubstantiated pieces of information to the detriment of our client without making an attempt to go through them as detailed a fashion as possible. That's number one. The second issue, Your Honour, is that what happens in this Chamber is not just for this Chamber. I appreciate Your Honours attention and your intuitiveness in this regard, but hopefully not. But it could very well that somebody else is going to have to -- going to have to read this particular transcript. The last thing is we are going to have to put together a trial brief on this where we cite to particular items in the evidence, not just what we consider to be Your Honours' conclusions in this regard, but the facts that were actually brought out and substantiated, such as, I know Your Honour didn't like the particular question, but there was method to what I was doing. When there is an unknown cause of death, we need to establish quite clearly and put it in the report that they cannot exclude natural causes. If they cannot exclude natural causes, they have not proven anything with regard to this death. Now, there are any number of these that are in this indictment, or in this clarification schedule. And what we are attempting to do is to address this as quickly as possible. Now I took a very, very minor period of time the other day, and I took less than a session the first time before Your Honour grew impatient with my questioning. Nevertheless as we move down the line, the questions that are given by not only Dr. Baccard, but also Clark, are going to be significant for any final trial brief when Your Honour has to consider exactly how to deal with these clarifications, these additional 189 killings that are in there, plus the ones that were in there from the first place. So the restriction on time in doing that, and Your Honour I took a very, very short period of time given amount of information, 53 autopsies that were presented by the Prosecution, that I objected to the restriction of that time on that basis. To make a record and to answer what the -- obviously the Prosecution has not answered itself, but it seeming like in this evidence shifting situation that we find ourselves, we have the Prosecution just dumping all this stuff out there on the floor, that they then turn to the Prosecution to sort out. That's what has happened here, and that's why it takes time, and it takes -- it is a little bit labourious, Judge, I agree with you, to go through with it, and maybe a little bit tedious, but it's necessary because there is no other way to answer this particular item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the reason why you were limited on time was based exclusively on the basis of how you used your time before, and in any later legal argument, you can rely on a report, which is, in many respects, perfectly clear, often without additional questions. We will ... Ms. Frolich, is the Prosecution ready to call Mr. Puhovski for being further examined?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Puhovski.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony is still binding. Mr. Misetic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning again, Professor.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We left off on Friday talking about the topic of your essay in August 1995. I wanted to ask you, I'm sure you're familiar with the subsequent situations in Eastern Slavonia, the peaceful transition of eastern Slavonia to Croatian authority. And the Trial Chamber earlier in this case heard evidence that 25 percent of the ethnic Serb population that lived in Eastern Slavonia prior to 1991 left between 1996 and 1998 rather than choosing to go stay to live in even Slavonia. As someone who was familiar with the processes that were taking place throughout this this time, do you have an understanding or an explanation as to why those people - and I'm talking exclusively of the 25 percent of the ethnic Serbia population that lived in even Slavonia prior to 1991 - why they would have left Eastern Slavonia even as it was being peacefully integrated?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my understanding they left Eastern Slavonia precisely due to the reintegration, whatever its character be, even the peaceful one, because they did not want to remain in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, in terms of the political authority there. That was the territory that had not, for several years, been under the authority of Croatia. On several occasions, I went to the area with Mr. Klein and I spoke to a number of these individuals. My estimation is, is that they lived there with a mixture of fear that had to do with propaganda and that to do with the information reaching the area once the columns reached Serbia from Sector South. These columns were used by the Serbian TV to divulge reports about it being impossible to live together with Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. Klein was the administrator of the UN transitional authority in Eastern Slavonia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Subsequent to the official turnover of authority in Eastern Slavonia to the authorities of the Republic of Croatia, were there killings, burnings, and other forms of physical violence toward the ethnic Serb community in Eastern Slavonia after the transition?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, there weren't any, and I believe that I would be aware of such a thing happening, had they happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just my last question on this topic area. I'm sure you're familiar with the departure of ethnic Serbs from Kosovo after NATO authority was established and their departure from the Sarajevo suburb of Ilidza after IFOR entered. Do you have any knowledge as to the reasons why those populations would have left?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have very little information and second-hand information at that. As far as I know, in the case of Kosovo, the Serbs believe that the NATO was an enemy administration which proved as such by having bombed their country; whereas I cannot tell you anything specific about Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Turning to a different topic, I want to go through some of these people that are identified in the report as having been killed during and after military Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can start off, this is ... Yes, it doesn't have a P number yet. It is the HHO report, which is 65 ter 4674, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can you say that number again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 65 ter 4674. And if we can go first to numbered page 142.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm taking you to killings in the Drnis area. This is in the village of Cerovac, C-e-r-o-v-a-c. And you see the two entries at 55 and 56 which are two brothers. Let me wait for the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, there are two different pages in the two versions shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At the bottom, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have found it. It's 135 in the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now you see here there's a report that a Branislav Dokic, born in 1963, was a disabled person, did not serve the army. During the military Operation Storm, the Croatian army took him outside the house and killed him. Number 56 is Dusan Dokic, Branislav's brother. "He was ill. The Croatian army took him too and promised to bring him back in two or three days." But he is also identified as killed in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Registrar if we could now have on the screen, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I would ask you to in number 55 to -- in both entries to keep in mind it says Ilinko as the father's name or mother's name, born in 1963, and then there's a brother Dusan, called Dusko, born in 1965.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have 1D67-0365 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now you will see that Branislav who was listed in the HHO report as having been killed during Operation Storm was in fact interviewed by the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And he was interviewed on the 17th of August, 1995. And if you look, his personal identifying information, father's name Ilija, and then he says he was born in 1963 which would match the year of birth in your report. Under other information at the bottom he says his mother is Ilinka, which is consistent with the name that appeared in the HHO report as Ilinka. He also references that he has a brother Dusan, born in 1965. And then if we were to read through this, he would indeed say he was not a member of the ARSK. But if we continue to see what happened to his brother ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D1311.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1311 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have on the screen please 1D67-0155.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now this is the report of the interview of Dusan Dokic. Again, if we turn the page, please, and you see this is taken on the 17th of August, and the personal identifying information is he is the son of Ilija; the date of birth is 1965; the remaining -- the other information again the mother's name is Ilinka. He references that he has a brother Branislav born in 1963. And then if you turn the page he talks about his participation in the ARSK army.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. President, if just one comment, also notes that the residence of these two individuals is Mrakovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, if there is anything you would like to draw the witness to, you can do that in re-examination. There is no need to complete perhaps a selective choice of what to draw attention to. That is up to Mr. Misetic to do it in his way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1312, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1312 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if I could now have Exhibit 1D67-0126 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm now showing you a decision by the president of the Republic of Croatia from the 30th of December, 1995, in which he decided to grant amnesty to certain members of the ARSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page. I have not translated just the relevant portion for this exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you see right there in the middle of the screen, Dusan Dokic, son of Ilija, born in 1965, against whom criminal proceedings are under way before the military court in Zagreb for the criminal offence of armed rebellion ... is freed from criminal prosecution. So based on your review of this documentation unless there is some incredible --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Split, not in Zagreb. The proceedings took place in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... right. Now, there is a mistake in the translation, and we will have to have that corrected. You see that, unless there is some incredible coincidence, that these two brothers in fact appear to have been alive, Branislav certainly as of 17th August and Dusan on 30th of December 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the two reports are not contradictory. We have received reports about people being taken away, which is true in this case. Some of them were interviewed; others were subject of criminal proceedings; and still others never returned home. As far as we know, the two individuals did not return home until 1998. That's why their neighbours listed them as persons who were missing, who had not returned. And that's what was noted down here. We didn't know what happened to them subsequently. I am glad to hear that they are alive. But I have no information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, actually that leads me into one of the one more overall points I wanted to talk to you about. Part of the information is, of course, based on if somebody is missing, you would rely on the stories that -- or the information that people who had been left behind would tell you about what happened to certain people. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And when it is it established that somebody returned two or three or six month the later, we would know about it because we would receive reports. The last time we went to check whether they returned was in 1997, and then we would check them against the list we had. If they hadn't returned, we would note down that unless they were registered elsewhere and we were able to receive the information from their friends, neighbours, or people who knew them, we would again need confirmation from two independent sources, we would conclude that they were dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit on the screen be marked and I tender it into evidence with the caveat that we will correct the mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1313, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1313 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There's another entry in the HHO report, which again is 65 ter 4674. It is in the English page 145. That's 145, which is page 146 in the B/C/S. It is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, 138.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 138. Thank you, Professor. It is entry -- person number 111.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One more page forward in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 139, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, one more page. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now -- number 111 is in Otric. It relates to an individual named Ilija Veselinovic, born December 8, 1931, found dead in the vicinity of the road Gracac-Otric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if I could have 1D67-0001, please. This would be at page 5 in the Croatian text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is -- what I'm going to show you, and we'll be referring back to occasionally. This is a report of an investigation done by the Croatian police, in part, that deals with part of -- of the HHO report. In other words, somebody filed a criminal complaint on the basis of the allegations made in the HHO report and the Croatian police, in 2002, reported to the state attorney's office as to what information the police had about some of the names that appear in the HHO report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So if we go to page 5, under entry number 1, it deals with Nikola Dragicevic, but it says towards the middle -- actually if you go down to the entry that says -- towards the middle of that second paragraph under Nikola Dragicevic, it says it was established that Ilija Veselinovic was a civilian. He was identified on the basis of the identity card number found on him, issued by Obrovac Municipal Secretariat of the Interior. If you go to the next paragraph it says. On 6 February 2001, the Obrovac police station issued personal identify card in the name of Ilija Veselinovic, son of Johan, born 5 October 1931. Subsequent investigation removed any doubt that this is one and the same person and that the date of birth was changed on the basis of the date found in the register of births. During an interview Ilija Veselinovic, he stated he lost his wallet in the night on the Gracac-Otric road when he left the Republic of Croatia during military and police Operation Storm. The wallet also contained his medical card and an identity card issued in his name. Then the report goes on to talk about who in fact may have picked up that identity card and who the person -- who the body might be. Now, with respect to Ilija Veselinovic, some of -- at least with respect to Ilija Veselinovic identified in the report, it turns out that that person born in 1931 in fact appears to have been alive as of 2002, and so some of the information in your report also can be mistaken on the basis of mistakes such as this, in terms of how a body was identified when it was found. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It cannot be contested that this was a mistake. A person whose was found who was an elderly man who had grey hair and had an identity card on him in the name of Ilija Veselinovic. It was under that name that he was buried, and the information was conveyed to everyone concerned. The new piece of information emerged in spring of 2001, and I got to know about it only two years later. Unfortunately, or fortunately the name was wrong, and as far as I know, to this day, the identity of the dead body has not been established. Even though this report claims to know the identity of the person, it was said that the person resided in Serbia, so undoubtedly he was killed in that area, and, undoubtedly the name that we wrote down and attributed to him was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just so -- you didn't get to see the second part of the report there. But it says that this body was found along with the bodies of eight other individuals, all of whom were members of the ARSK army. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the gentleman -- it was not that gentleman, because, first, it was said that this was the name of the gentleman, but then later on it was established that the person under that name resides in Belgrade, so this individual is still unknown. And let me say that there were more individuals found who were soldiers and who were not identified in this report because, undoubtedly, they were members of a military group.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, Ms. Frolich, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1314, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, we have this whole report. You gave examples where there's a clear -- on the basis of the other documents you have shown, at least there's a very strong support for the suggestion that they're still alive. At least were still alive at a certain moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, and could you perhaps agree with Ms. Frolich on how many are established to be still alive. I mean, that's, of course, important information for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would be happy to do it outside of the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll hear later from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Happy to discuss it, yeah. If we could turn to the next page which is page 146 in the English. It's entry number 120 in the report. I'm sorry, I have the wrong exhibit on the screen. 65 ter 4674, which is page 140 in the B/C/S; e-court page 140 in the B/C/S, yes. Okay. If we look at -- it's actually the one on the bottom, 120. I don't know why we have ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have several entries, 120. I don't know whether you want to refer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Djuro Mandic or Djuro Cenic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's what got me confused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 140 of the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There seems to be a mis-numbering, Professor, which through me off. It should be 120 in the English, Djuro Mandic. That's the person I wanted to ask you about. You see there that the allegation in the report that he was 81 years old, that he was slaughtered and massacred in his backyard around August 20th. Firstly, he was buried in the backyard. Then his body was moved to Gracac under the number 387 but without the name on it. And at the time of this incident, the Croatian Helsinki Committee actually filed a public report which I'd like to show you, which is 1D67-0055, which is an HHO statement number 29, dated on the 2nd of November, 1999, put out by the president, Ivan Zvonimir Cicak. You can see statement number 29, and if we go to page 2 in the B/C/S, and page 3 in the English. The incident with Djuro Mandic is the fourth paragraph from the bottom in the Croatian version. And it's in the middle of the page there in the English. It says: "Djuro Mandic was massacred in this courtyard on August 25, 1995. At that time his head and both of his arms were cut off, and traces of brutal torture were visible on his body. Close relatives buried him there, but when they requested that he be buried in the local cemetery, members of the MUP took the body and without their permission or presence allegedly buried him in Gracac." The last page has the -- states that it is issued by the President, Ivan Zvonimir Cicak, and it's dated 2nd November 1995. Mr. President, if I could ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1315, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, if we could have 1D67. Again, sorry, that was just admitted. It's 1D67-0001; I'm just looking for the D number, as it was just admitted. D1314, Mr. Registrar. It's numbered page 21 in the Croatian, and numbered page 20 in the English. It's at the top, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, it list what the allegation is. In the first sentence it says, this is again that report by the Ministry of Interior in 2002. It says Djuro Mandic 81, slaughtered and massacred. I think it should be 25 July -- 20 August, I'm sorry, again, there is a wrong date, and we will have to correct that. "... in his courtyard and buried in Gracac."

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. In Croatian it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Then the MUP reports on what information it has about this incident. And it says: "In 2002 the MUP reports Marija Mandic, daughter of Djuro, born on such-and-such a date, went to the Gracac police station on 9 September 1995 to report that on 25 August 1995, she had found her father Djuro Mandic death dead in the garden of their home. She buried her father but now wants to move him to the Gracac town cemetery. The remains of Djuro Mandic, whose real name is Georgije Mandic, were buried at Gracac cemetery following the guidelines for the humane disposal of bodies?" And finally, let me show you a Prosecution document which is P1355. This is the Croatian protocol, and this will show you a picture of the body as buried. And I had ask you to remember to Mr. Cicak's report that Mr. Mandic's head and arms were cut off. Now, that's the picture that's been identified as Georgije Mandic, but you can see that it appears that his head and arms were in fact not cut off. And if we turn the page, you can see that this is the autopsy -- or the identification for -- in fact Georgije Mandic. Now can you explain how the HHO came into information that in fact this person had been massacred and his head and arms had been cut off?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From his family. They shared that with our associates. By that time, that piece of information had been published, and it wasn't put into question. I don't know whether this is the picture of the very corpse. What is important is that he was killed, buried in his yard, and then moved elsewhere. Those were the facts we came forward with. They are not in dispute. As for whether his arms and head were cut off, that's something I can't tell you. We received that information, and we published it. It was not denied until 2001, although we can see that the police had had some reports prior to that, but for some reasons of their own, they wouldn't share it. We were unable to get by those reports, and we published what we had. What I can tell you is that this was not denied by the time Mr. Cicak's statement reached the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. My question to you is in terms of the -- your now review of the investigation conducted by the HHO, do you agree that sometimes information provided by relatives might not necessarily be accurate such as if in fact the information came from the relative that the arms and head were cut off, that sometimes that information it be exaggerated?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, unfortunately. I only want to say that in the last two days there were seven instances of misinformation that you and Ms. Higgins operated with. You have had a lot of information at your disposal, our reports, expert reports, and still you make mistakes. You can only imagine what the situation was like for us in 1995 and 1996; that's to say how our colleagues had to work in the field without any prior or additional information whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me turn your attention to pages 25 and 26 of 65 ter 4674 which is the HHO report, and I'm referring again, unfortunately, to the English pages.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's an entry in the back at number 140 for Asija Delic, but this is in the actual report itself. You give more detail about what happened to her and her family. And I'd like to ask you a few questions about this. But this is the paragraph that begins: "126 residents lived ..." And then towards the middle it says: "Only four persons remained to live in the village. The Delic family, mother Saja" -- and this is page, yes, 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yeah, page 24 in the Croatian version. "The Delic family, mother Saja, born in 1904, her son Donaj, his wife Bosilka, and the old women Saja Barac." And then the next paragraph says: "The soldiers belonging to the 5th Corps of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian army entered the villages of Nebrusi [phoen] and Kruge [phoen] without any fight at all. The Croatian army entered on 7 August. The soldiers of the Bosnian-Herzegovina army entered the village of Nebrusi on August 3rd. The Delic family was literally destroyed that day. If we go down it says: "Mother Saja disappeared and Bosilijka was found with serious bodily injures. She was transferred to Bosnia with the help of some international humanitarian organizations. We turn the page in English, and we can stay on this page in the Croatian. "The mother Saja Delic was hospitalised in Knin where she died from the consequences of beating on December 21, 1995." Now, from this story it would appear that in fact this woman and some members of her family were beaten by members of the 5th Corps of the ABiH which entered certain areas of Croatia first. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what we received by way of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a different report on this topic of the ABiH, which is 1D67-0369, please. This is a police interview from 2002 with a woman named Danica Leka. She talks about what happened to her.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. President, I thought the procedure was to first put the question to the witness from an interview, even if it is an Official Note than show the actual note.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's not the practice that's been thus far, Mr. President. It has been OTP statements and matters that have been given to the OTP. Plus, the individuals I'm talking about are in his report, so in effect, there is no difference between this and a police note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, before showing a witness, it is always good to see whether he has any spontaneous recollection of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Without looking at the document, Professor, I'm going take you through the exercise of the formality. What happened to Nikola Babic, Rade Babic, Nikola Oric, Oleg Pavolic? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's go to the document then. This is a note of the police interview of Danica Leka. And if we could put that up. Now, if you go to the fourth paragraph, she says that her son, Nedeljko, and this is Nedeljko Leka, who is entry number 354 in the HHO report at page 161 in the English, "had gone missing 5 August 1995. According to her information, members of the 5th Corps Bosnian army had breached that border area of the Republic of Croatia in BH and immediately prior to his disappearance, and it goes on, according to her information, her son was killed by members of the B and H army, as it is known that they were in the area at that time and not members of the HV. She disposes" -- and now there's a translation error here. If you look at the original, it says: "She disposes of information that members of the 5th Corps killed some additional persons of Serb ethnic origin." And there is reference to a Petar Babic in the original which was not translated into the English. Petar Babic is in the HHO report at entry 346. And then it goes on, such as Rada Babic, who is line 347 in the HHO report, born in 1936. She goes on -- I'll skip some of these individuals who are not in the report. Then Nikola Babic, called Niko, from Arapovdol [phoen] who was a civilian, after he refused to give him his horse; and Nikola Orlic, who is entry 349 in the HHO report at page 161, son of Dragan, born 1928, a member of the army of the RSK who was armed while conducting guard duty at the Abdic mountain in civilian clothing. According to her information, members of the 5th corps of the ABiH army killed Oleg Pavlovic. Oleg Pavlovic is entry 350 in the HHO report at page 161 in the English. My question is, it is legitimate because your report doesn't apparently distinguish between whether someone was killed by the Bosnian army or the Croatian army. So in fact these people were killed, and it is accurate to predict -- to portray that in the report. My question to you, though, is in term it is of the persons killed, some of these individuals, or the person doing the killing in fact in quite a few of these incidents, were in fact from the Bosnian army 5th Corps. Do you have any personal knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we had Petar and Rade as Bobics, not Babics. Therefore, on our list the last name was Bobic. However, it seems that this refers to the same situation. Second of all, we didn't find it within our remit to accuse anyone. We are an NGO. We did our best to establish who the victims were and, if possible, if we knew, we stated which units were present in the field at the time. As I said on Friday, we had some information about the people who were killed by a RSK plane. We also have some information based on the reports of the people killed by members of the 5th Corps, in some ten locations. We also have information on the whereabouts of certain Croatian units, when some murders took place. All that information was provided, and we received it through witness reports. Our task was not to allocate responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1316, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1316 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we're close to a break, but I was asked to put on the record that the Gotovina Defence has tendered a bar table submission that were leftover documents from the cross-examination of Witness Lausic, as well as from the summer witness Roberts, and the Prosecution has indicated no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, have numbers already been assigned to them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that these bar table exhibits were presented in a format as the Chamber asked for, which is very much appreciated. Mr. Registrar, would you please prepare a list and provisionally assign exhibit numbers so that the Chamber can decide on the admission. Then we'll have a break. We will resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, before we continue, I'd like to very briefly with a procedural matter. We have received a new motion in relation to Witness 82. Same request, grounds now different; videolink. The Chamber would like to hear as soon as possible from the parties whether there are any objections against this new motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We will be objecting. If you wish, we'll file something in writing, or if you wish to hear it orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we could hear it orally, but perhaps we then -- it's clear to us, and let's see whether we still find time. How much time would it take?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: For me, 60 seconds, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sixty seconds, yes. Other Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will object as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to review the filing this afternoon and inform the Court this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic. Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I beg your pardon, but I just wanted to briefly address the bar table for Witness Lausic. We didn't have a chance to make our comments before the break. We just briefly wanted to say there are no objections to all documents aside from the video-clip that -- excuse me, that we have been unable to view the video-clip until now. That is Document 1D66-0252, and if possible we want it reserved until we have had the chance to view it, which would probably be, maybe even during this session. And another comment I wanted to make on document that was submitted on tab 4 of the Defence chart which was 1D66-0001 examples of the mobilised HV members against whom legal proceedings were taken. We don't object to the documents themselves, but we wanted to put on the record that that description does represent accurately what is contained in these document, since not all service records show that indeed these members against whom criminal reports are filed were demobilized at the time that the crime was commit -- the crime in question was committed, or at least it is unclear in some instances what these records show. We can send a more detailed review to the Chamber if that would be of assistance or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course what the Chamber would prefer that if we're just talking about characterizing what the document is, that if the parties could agree on that, that would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. I can just tell the Prosecution that it is either they were demobilized as a result of the criminal activity, or in the MUP report, they are identified as members of the HV when in fact they were demobilized well prior to that. So either way, it was submitted for both purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... At least the report, it is demobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If my description could be amended to show at which point they demobilised at in relation to the crime -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's not spend too much time in Court on what seems to be a matter of relatively small importance. And if the parties need any assistance in uniting on the description, I make myself available to assist. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I next wish to turn to the person identified as victim number 64 in the report, and this is on page 142 in the English, and her name is Marija Puskar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if I could cull up 1D67-0111, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, the report at entry 64 identifies Marija Puskar as being a Serb born in 1928. And if we look at -- I'll show you two documents. First this is a report prepared on 10th of August, this is an official police note on the discovery of the body, and can you see that a Milan Mujan entered the premises on the 7th of August and found Marija Puskar hanging in the house. It says he said that he was familiar with the fact that the husband Nikola and sons Jovo, Mile, and Bosko, were members of paramilitary units and extremists individuals, maltreated the deceased in the manner that they physically abused her, beat her, and it says that they cursed her Ustasha mother. Before I get to the next note, Mr. President, if I ask that this exhibit be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1317, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1317 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could now go to 1D67-0113, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is again on the 10th August, and I'm just interested here in the first paragraph. It says it's compiled in the Drnis police station. In connection with the suicide by hanging of Marija Puskar, maiden name Mujan where she was also residing. She was a housewife by occupation, Croat by origin. Now, how did the HHO -- my question is how did the HHO go about identifying the ethnicity of some of the individuals who were identified as being killed?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like any other data, we received this information based on the statement of her relatives, family, or neighbours, anyone who could provide us with information on the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The next question is if someone committed suicide, would the HHO have considered that person to have been killed, such that they would then be included in the report?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the report, I believe there are five or six references to suicide. They are separated from the rest. We had information on those few people as having killed themselves. We put them in a separate category, stating that probably because of the situation at the time, they decided to kill themselves. However, we did not have information on this woman killing herself, and we did not have the information contained in this report that she was an ethnic Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1318, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Staying on the topic of suicides, there is an entry five lines above the Marija Puskar entry for Grozdana Sepelj at entry 59, unknown nationality, the corpse was found on 6 August in Drnis. She was buried in Sibenik. 1D67-0107, please, Mr. Registrar. Yes, 1D67-0107.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may caution to something. The reference to her son and husband being killed during the liberation of Zitnic, that is not correct. The son is still among the living. Hence, there are mistakes on each page or -- by each of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I think the report said that the sons and the father, the earlier report we saw, fled towards Knin and left her in the house, but we can check that.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says deceased. And then there is no dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the record of external examination of Grozdana Sepelj taken 7 August 1995, and it says she was born in 1958.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in both the English and the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to apologise, Professor, in the Croatian, the copy we have is very bad due to the photocopying.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The conclusion on the 7th of August is from the obtained information: "And after conducting examination my conclusion is that this is a suicide case by an explosive device, and that the above mentioned amputations and injuries to the head region caused death." How many -- when you were conducting your analysis, did you include individuals who either, for example, died as a result of an explosion of a device they, themselves, were carrying, or for example, another possibility is people who were travelling off of main roads who may have come across land-mines and things like that. Would those people be people that would be included in your report as having been killed?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To repeat, we included in the report those whose murder was confirmed by at least two people. I can only warn you of the following, as any expert might. A suicide committed by a woman by using a hand-grenade is something that simply does not exist in Croatia and such environs. I don't believe that is reason enough to believe that she had committed suicide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes people accidentally kill themselves, right? They don't intend to die, but if they're handling explosive devices improperly, they can wind up killing themselves. Correct? My question to you is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm merely reacting to what I see. In my view, this conclusion is not founded on the material facts. Perhaps it should have stated "accident." There were explosives all over the place at the time, and laypeople handled it. That is not in dispute. Perhaps they should have said that she was toying around with the explosive or trying to do something with it, thus killing herself. That I would find reasonable. But this is a bit far-fetched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, to follow up on one of your answers, and it may be an issue in the English terminology, but you said that you, I believe, consider these to be murders. And the title of Annex 1 is civilians killed during and after Operation Storm. And I you're not -- I don't have any knowledge that you are a lawyer. You may have some legal training, but if you do, please correct me. But there is a distinction that you may know between someone being killed and someone being murdered. And I guess if you can clarify for us now this annex, is it an annex of people who were killed; or an annex of people that the Croatian Helsinki Committee contends were murdered?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information we had, and I stress again that we received that information from the people who certainly did not possess such expert knowledge, we received information on people being killed, being outside the area of combat. I would say then perhaps that such people were killed without participating in combat, and on the basis of such information, we cited those persons in the report, following witness statements in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm sorry, if this is repetitive, but I just want to clarify this. If a person or a group of people travelling along come across and trigger a land-mine, for example, and one or more of them are killed, is that the type of individual or individuals who would be considered as -- who would be considered as inclusive in this report, or would you exclude those people this report?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in one place are two persons mentioned as having been killed by explosives. One of them was a victim of a booby-trap that was planned in a house; and the other individual was killed by a shell in the yard. This was part of the description of how they met their end, and this was killing. It was not part of what we wanted to base our report on, based on the accounts we heard in the field, about people being murdered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit on the screen be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D1319, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The next person that we wish -- I wish to ask you about is at -- is at line 86, or is the person identified as 86, which is page 144 in the English, page 139 in the B/C/S, and this is Marija Banjanin.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 138 in my version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I mean 139 in the e-court version of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The electronic version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And Mr. -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can just read it out. That's fine. You have it in front of you, Professor, so it says at entry 86: "She was found without a head." It says "he," it should be: "She was last seen --" or "was seen last time on 6 August 1995 in front of the police station in Gracac."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could call up 1D67-0115, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. In my report it only says a Serb lady, aged 89, found -- she was a bedridden, disabled person found in her bed. There is nothing else that's mentioned in my report. The book is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at the English translation, sir, so ...

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. We were responsible for the English translation, but this is what the original states, and in that case it's an error on our part, since we're responsible for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm actually more interested in the part that she was found without a head, so I think we're consistent with the English and the Croatian on that point. This is the --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the Official Note of the discovery of her body, and it says that they -- the police in the second paragraph arrived at the site of the incident. The daughter was there, Radmila Banjanin, and said that inside the house she found her mother Marija Banjanin, born in 1905, no other information, dead in the bedroom next to the bed. "After examining the site of the incident, it was established that the body of the female person, examination conducted in the presence of the physician on duty, Ivan Perovic ... was approximately two weeks old." Talks about objects were scattered across the room. Next paragraph: "We secured the site of the incident until the arrival of the investigation team ... when the investigating judge of the county court of the Zadar-Knin country, Petric Milan, arrived at the site ..." as well as operative officers, criminal technicians, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1320, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence. Mr. Misetic, if the English version differs from the original one, then, of course, it's a matter on which the Chamber would like to be informed, even if the witness accepts responsibility for an English translation which is not accurate. Nevertheless, I do understand that this is not because he accepts responsibility for the new text but for a mistake being made in translating the original text. Is that how I understand your testimony? That means that, of course, the Chamber would like to have the original --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you inform the Chamber where the differences exactly are because you mentioned something about being found without a head, and that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's in both the -- -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's in both. Yes, of course, I'm not in a position because the witness commented on the original version. So I do understand that that's found in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could now go back to D1314, please. And this is page 12 of the English -- sorry, page 12 of the Croatian and page 12 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is under Gracac. It says Marija Banjanin. This is, again, that police report from 2002 which tried to investigated some of the allegations in the report. It says: Marija Banjanin, born in 1906, disabled, her head was cut off. And then it talks again. It repeats some of the information we've seen, that the body was found by the daughter. The investigating judge of Zadar county court and officers of Zadar police administration went on location. An autopsy was carried out on the body of Marija Banjanin by a pathologist who established that she had died of natural causes. The discovery -- they discovered that the corpse was about 20 days old. We have sent you a special report concerning the above.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can tell you, Mr. President, we don't have a copy of the special report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But, Professor, you would agree with me that if in fact she died of natural causes, then -- and nothing in the report of the on-site location indicates that the body -- or the head had been severed from the body. Would this be another report that was based on information that you had heard as opposed to information that would have been independently verified by an examination of the body?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat again: We weren't able to receive any sort of police reports at the time, though we sought them. This information was made public at a much later date. We published the information we had. Let me just note that in the first report it stated that the body was 14 days old; in the second report, it is stated that it was 20 days old. Evidently, the job was not done that professionally. I'm sorry if we received inaccurate information. I repeat, that was the only information we had. We sought a response from all the different police stations in relation to the information we had, and I repeat, if there are inconsistencies or inaccuracies in the report, they stem from the lack of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then let me turn your attention to two other -- two entries in the report. One is at line 62, which is page 142 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's e-court 137 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's an entry is a says Draginja Vukse, Serb, killed. The corpse was found in the well. And then if you turn to page 152, at the entry at number 218, it says: "Dragica Vukse, Serb, old, between 90 and 95. She was found in a well on November 13, 1995." Now, my question to you is, are you familiar with the possibilities of double-counting in your reports the same person because the first name -- let me put it to you. Draginja and Dragica can be variations of the same first name; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that is highly likely. I'm not certain of it, but it is quite likely that this is indeed the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And let me just show you the police report of the discovery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 1D67-0149, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And This is the special report when the body was discovered. And again, this is consistent with the entry in one of the entries which says that the body was found on 13 -- sorry, 11 November 1995. It says an investigative judge went out on the 13th of November; conducted a on-site investigation. Members of UNCIVPOL were present. A crime technician examined and photographed the site. Now the paragraph below I wanted to ask you about because it says: "Members of the UNCIVPOL stated that they received information about the incident from members of the Dalmatian Solidarity Committee from Split Mr. Ivica Vojko and Mrs. Olja Simic who discovered the body in a well and found that it was the body of Draginja Vukse who they were trying to locate for sometime, since 19 September 1995." Now, this -- it says Olja Simic. Is that really Olga Simic, who was also in the Croatian Helsinki Committee?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. This was her nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When members of the Croatian Helsinki Committee would find a body, was it typical that they would first contact the international monitors in the area without contacting the police, or how would they go about contacting members of the police to investigate?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how it worked in practice. At first, we wanted some of their relatives or neighbours to report that to the police, since our experience and cooperation with the police on the ground was quite poor. If that wasn't possible, then our activists would go to the police, and if that didn't work either, then we would turn to some of the international representatives present in the area. This was the practice we agreed upon after our first field visit, where it turned out that our contacts with the police did not work that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, it says, remarking on the result of the physical examination, it says that: "Dr. Josip Dujella, a specialist pathologist, conducted the external physical examination ... the examination was conducted during the on-site investigation, at which point the specialist pathologist established that there were no visible signs of violence on the body and established the cause of death as drowning." Beneath that, it says: "There are no indications pointing towards a criminal offence." Now, would -- first, did the Croatian Helsinki Committee know of the results of the investigation by the investigating judge and the special pathologist before it included the name of --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They always treated us as an organisation that was not entitled to special information. That is why we tried to have family members report such incidents because they would be entitled to further information. As far as I know, we did not receive this or any other police reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree with me that with respect to many of the entries in the report, in order to verify what actually happened in terms of the results of an investigation, we would have to actually go to the MUP records for each incident and see whether an examination was conducted and whether there were results of any investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I repeat, had we been able to gain access to them. This is a NGO report, a report by a NGO, which is not engaged in any activities related to criminology but in establishing victims. There is one thing called the pathological examination of the site. This is something that is not the typical practice in civilised countries, although it proved necessary in the countries at war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D1321.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit D1321 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, rather than go through a lot of these, I think I'm satisfied with the answers of the professor, and I will just bar table which respect to some of the other incidents, for which I expect that there will be similar answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: There is no objection to similar documents. Yeah, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we can compare the content of these documents with the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber waits for bar table submissions in relation to the other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Turning your attention to an exhibit that the Prosecution admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is P2319, MFI, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the Feral Tribune article you gave some testimony on under examination by Ms. Frolich about, and in your testimony, you mentioned, if I'm not mistaken, that you were present when Mr. Mrkalj, who is the subject of the interview, was speaking to the journalist; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was present only at the point when he discussed the final version and tried to prevent his interview from being shortened. I did not attend the interview itself, only his -- I was only present when he talked to the journalist who wanted to cut the interview short, whereas Mr. Mrkalj wanted to have certain things that he believed were important added to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you gain -- come to understand or learn as to why the journalist wanted to cut the information?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was reassuring Mr. Mrkalj about the -- the fact that the space that had been given to him in the Feral Tribune weekly was already extensive and that they could not afford to give him any more space than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever come to learn the circumstances around -- surrounding which how this interview came to be published?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you have anything to do with the agreement between Mr. Mrkalj and the journalist to conduct this interview?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have any contacts with the people from Feral Tribune. It was Mr. Cicak who dealt with that. I said that by that time, the texts by Mr. Cicak and Banac already been published, and then Mr. Mrkalj's interview was published, and a week later I think it was my London text that you asked me a couple of questions about that was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Vjeran Grkovic is a journalist who would accurately report Mr. Mrkalj's words?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell. I don't know much about Mr. Grkovic. When I read the interview, it seemed to be consistent with the way in which Mr. Mrkalj spoke, and I believe that Mr. Mrkalj was content with the published interview, save for two details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You say you don't know much about Mr. Grkovic. Do you know anything about him?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing, expect for the fact that he was a Feral Tribune journalist for a period of time and that two or three years subsequent to this interview being published, he no longer emerged as one of the contributors to that weekly. I don't know what his occupation is today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could put on the screen -- actually, we'll put it up via Sanction, 1D67-0254, please. I'm sorry. We can show it in e-court. I apologise. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who is Drago Pilsel?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago Pilsel is a pretty well-known Croatian journalist who was a member of the Croatian Helsinki Committee for a number of years and today contributes mostly to the Novi List.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And he was one of the HHO activists in the field in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the field on this one occasion, and he published a report on this -- in Novi List.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 4 of Mr. Pilsel's statement to the OTP, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know what the question is going to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither do I.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I put it to him already, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's, of course, we ... Please proceed, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to paragraph 24, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pilsel told the OTP: "During this period, I also published under a shared pseudonym, Vjeran Grkovic, in other newspapers. At the time, my paper was not prepared to publish some of the articles that I was producing." Now, Mr. Puhovski, did you know that the Feral Tribune article that the Prosecution is tendering is in fact written by Dragan Pilsel under the pseudonym Vjeran Grkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I hear of it or I read of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, interestingly, in the Feral Tribune article Mr. Pilsel makes reference to himself and meetings he had with Mr. Pasic. Of course, he's writing about himself under a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, obviously, I can see that this comes as a surprise to you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. [Interpretation] I know that Mr. Pilsel had difficulties in the Novi List; I'm aware of that. I also know of another pseudonym that he used to publish texts. I was not aware of this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, it would appear that this article was in fact written in agreement within the Croatian Helsinki Committee. In other words, Mr. Pilsel and Mr. Mrkalj within the HHO agreed to publish this in the form of an interview. Do you know anything about the circumstances of the agreement between these two individuals as to what was going to be published?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat what I said on the first day of my testimony in response to Ms. Frolich. It was an agreement between Mr. Cicak and the editor-in-chief of the paper to have several articles published. That's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll move on, and we'll come back to Mr. -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, not being a native-speaking -- not native speaker, what is a shared pseudonym? Shared with whom? What?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it came to my mind, but perhaps -- apparently this witness can tell us anything about a shared pseudonym. From what I know from the English language, it might be an indication that several persons used that same pseudonym. That's, at least, if you share something with another person, that comes to my mind first. I can't think of any other -- I don't know whether the original of this or whether the tape is still there, so that we better understand what we find in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is why I'd asked that the exhibit be MFI'd, the Feral Tribune article. I wanted to make a submission on this point because, in fact -- I don't know if I should do this in private session or not, but -- I can tell you in 30 seconds, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think, as a matter of fact, there was another matter for which you needed 60 seconds, so let's do it at the end of this session. Then we have one and a half seconds. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could just go back so that when we pick up on this tomorrow it's fresh in our minds and we don't have to call this up again. If we can go back to the cover page of this, which is the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just -- I ask you to keep in mind the name he uses, which is also Carlos Zvonimir, and that will be relevant to tomorrow when we pick up on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, if you are going to new area, then I think the 90 seconds and a few matters might take altogether 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One of the matters I would like to raise is, how much time do you think you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll be done -- I had asked for an hour, and I'll try to keep it to 45 minutes or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still to go, 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I suppose you're aiming at me, Your Honour. I wouldn't have more than two sessions, maybe less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I'm thinking on how much time altogether. We cannot say that we made any promise, but at least we would try to accommodate this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think Mr. Mikulicic and I will talk, and I'll try to make sure that we take care of our portion in time so that the witness can leave tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes. I will endeavor to give him only a very short redirect, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the three of you could get together so that we could take care that, that the expectations of the witness are met. Do I understand well at the same time that the witness in line is not expected to start testimony tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Puhovski, we'd like to see you back tomorrow, and you have heard from the parties that -- well, they never used the word "promise," but there is a firm commitment to make sure that you can travel home again tomorrow, if, at least, your travel arrangements are adapted, and may I take it that this has been discussed with VWS. Then I again instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony, the testimony either already given or still to be given tomorrow. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Puhovski out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know to what extent it's proper to deal with the latest video-link motion in open session. Of course, it's of a --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Again, an abundance of caution, we should go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, 17th of February, at 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom I.
